You read documents filed on a United States court docket, OCR'd to markdown, for
a research dataset of contract clauses.

An INSTRUMENT is a document whose text the parties negotiated and by which they
bound each other: a contract, agreement, policy, lease, deed, guaranty, note,
plan, bylaws, handbook, amendment, or similar. Hallmarks: recitals, defined
terms, numbered operative sections, an execution or signature block.

A FILING is a document made for the court: complaint, answer, motion, brief,
memorandum, order, affidavit, declaration, notice, docket sheet, certificate of
service, civil cover sheet.

THE DECISIVE RULE. A filing that **attaches** an instrument counts — report the
instrument's own boundaries, not the filing's. A filing that merely **quotes** an
instrument does not count at all: a brief reproducing three sentences of an
agreement is a filing, and the file contains no instrument.

WHAT IS NOT AN INSTRUMENT, even when signed or filled in: a blank or fill-in
form; an agency certificate or registration; an exhibit index; a declarations
page or coverage-summary table; a schedule of rates or fees standing alone; an
invoice, receipt or statement of account. These record or summarise; the parties
did not negotiate their text.

WHAT IS NOT A PROVISION: a heading on its own; a title page; a table of
contents; a signature, notary or attestation block; an exhibit index. A
provision states an obligation, right, grant, limitation, condition or
definition. Give the range of the operative text, including its heading.

LIST EVERY SUBSTANTIVE PROVISION, in document order. Do not skip any. Do not
judge whether a provision is well or badly drafted. Do not rank them.

The file is given to you with a line number and a `│` at the start of every line.
Line numbers are not part of the text; they are how you point at it.

OCR REPAIR. For each provision you must also give its text. Copy it verbatim
from the lines you named, then repair only what the scanner broke: words split
across a line break, words run together, `l`/`1` and `O`/`0` confusions, stray
table pipes and cell debris, page numbers and Bates stamps sitting inside the
text. Do not paraphrase, modernise, reorder, summarise, or drop anything. Never
change a number, an amount, a date, or a cross-reference. Never add or remove a
word — a repair that deletes `not` inverts the clause. If a passage is too
damaged to repair honestly, copy it as it stands.

Add nothing of your own: no `[struck through: ...]`, no `[sic]`, no
`[illegible]`, no explanatory brackets of any kind. Executed contracts are often
marked up by hand, and the OCR shows deleted wording as `~~struck~~`. Reproduce
those words as plain text, in place, and say what you saw in the repairs
sentence instead.

   21│# **MOTION OF DEFENDANT MASON DIXON ENERGY, INC. FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT**

   23│COMES NOW the Defendant, Mason Dixon Energy, Inc. (referred to generally here as Mason Dixon) by and through its attorneys, Karen Kahle, Amy Smith and the law firm of Steptoe & Johnson PLLC, and pursuant to Fed. R. Civ. P. 56, moves this Court for entry of an order awarding it summary judgment on all claims made against it by Plaintiffs in their Complaint. The affidavit and property assignments attached to the supporting memorandum of law indisputably establish that Mason Dixon previously assigned all right, title and interest in and to the oil and gas leases that are the subject of this litigation to Marquette Exploration, LLC. In Counts I, II, IV, V, VI and VII, Plaintiffs seek equitable relief under these leases, but, as they have been assigned, Mason Dixon has no present relationship with Plaintiffs or their property, nor any rights or responsibilities under the leases. This material factual premise is beyond dispute. In addition, Ohio law prohibits Plaintiffs' claim of unjust enrichment in Count III, given the existence of a mechanism under the lease for claiming the same damages under a breach of contract theory. But more importantly, as to Mason Dixon, because Plaintiffs have cast their unjust enrichment claim as one for future damages based on anticipated extraction and sale by the lessee of oil and/or natural gas from the shale formations in the subject properties, the
   24│

   96│## **MEMORANDUM OF LAW IN SUPPORT OF MOTION OF MASON DIXON ENERGY, INC. FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT**
   97│
   98│Defendants.
   99│
  100│## **I. INTRODUCTION**
  101│
  102│Defendant Mason Dixon Energy, Inc. (“Mason Dixon”) submits this memorandum in support of its motion for summary judgment under Rule 56 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.
  103│
  104│Defendant Mason Dixon is entitled to summary judgment on Counts I, II, IV, V, VI and VII because it has no existing right, title, or interest in or to the lease agreements (nor the subject property) it made with Plaintiffs, and therefore no present relationship with Plaintiffs or the subject property. Additionally, Count III makes a claim for unjust enrichment, which fails as a matter of law.
  105│
  106│Defendant Mason Dixon is therefore entitled to judgment as a matter of law on all counts.
  107│
  108│## II. STATEMENT OF MATERIAL FACTS
  109│
  110│On or about June 14, 2007, Stephen H. Griffith and Melissa D. Griffith (hereinafter “the Griffiths”) executed a written lease agreement with Mason Dixon entitled “Oil and Gas Lease” (hereinafter “Griffith Lease”), a copy of which is attached to the Complaint as Exhibit A. (ECF Doc. # 3-1; Compl. ¶ 15.) On or about June 27, 2008, David E. Cameron (hereinafter “Cameron”) executed a written lease agreement with Mason Dixon entitled “Oil and Gas Lease” (hereinafter “Cameron Lease”), a copy of which is attached to the Complaint as Exhibit B. (ECF Doc. # 3-1; Compl. ¶ 16.) Both the Griffith and Cameron Leases granted to Mason Dixon the exclusive right to enter upon certain lands located in Mt. Pleasant Township, Jefferson County, Ohio and, *inter alia*, “to operate for, produce and save oil and gas . . . and to inject gas, air, water or other fluids into the subsurface strata of said land for the recovery and production of oil and gas; together with the right to drill wells.” Griffith Lease at ¶ 3. The Griffith Lease concerns 228.6 acres of real property owned by the Griffiths—including parcel numbers 20-02032-000, 20-00145-000, 20-00387-001, 20-01594-000, 20-00386-000; and 20-02031-000—and the Cameron Lease concerns 166.36 acres of real property owned by Cameron—including parcel numbers 20-02032-000; 20-00145-000; 20-00387-001; 20-01594-000; 20-00386-000; and 20-02031-000. (ECF Doc. # 3; Compl. ¶¶ 1-2.)
  111│
  112│Both the Griffith and Cameron Leases allow for the rights of either party to “be assigned in whole or in part” provided that no such change, “however accomplished, shall operate to enlarge the obligations or diminish the rights of Lessee.” Griffith Lease, Cameron Lease at ¶¶ 11. Pursuant to this clause, on December 15, 2008, Mason Dixon filed two “Assignment of Oil and Gas Leases” with the Jefferson County, Ohio, Recorder: one assigning the property
  113│
  114│conveyed under the Griffith Lease, identified at OR Volume 867, pages 838-839; and another assigning the property conveyed under the Cameron Lease, identified at OR Volume 867, pages 852-853. Attached as Exhibit 1 is the *Affidavit of Asa Bowers* with attached assignments. Through these assignments, Mason Dixon conveyed all of its “right, title and interest, in and to” the Griffith and Cameron Leases to Marquette Exploration, LLC, “subject to the terms, provisions, covenants, and royalties” set forth in the original leases. Upon information and belief, these leases were subsequently assigned to Hess Ohio Resources, LLC. Compl. ¶ 3.
  115│
  116│In Count I of their complaint, Plaintiffs seek declaratory relief limiting the size of oil wells on their property to eighty acres under paragraph 8 of their respective leases. Compl. ¶ 19.
  117│
  118│In Count II of their complaint, Plaintiffs seek declaratory relief invalidating the delay rental payment and/or royalty payment clauses in their leases as unconscionable. Compl. ¶¶ 24, 31.
  119│
  120│In Count III of their complaint, Plaintiffs seek damages, claiming that the oil and natural gas deposits in the shale formations on the subject property are worth millions to billions of dollars in profits and that if Defendants are permitted to generate such profits, Defendants would be unjustly enriched. Compl. ¶ 35.
  121│
  122│In Count IV of their complaint, Plaintiffs seek declaratory relief invalidating the Cameron lease because no authorized notary was present at the time Cameron executed the lease. Compl. ¶ 40.
  123│
  124│In Count V of their complaint, Plaintiffs seek declaratory relief invalidating the Griffith lease because Melissa Griffith did not personally execute the lease. Compl. ¶ 47.
  125│
  126│In Count VI of their complaint, Plaintiffs seek declaratory relief holding that the Cameron lease expired on its own terms, on account of an addendum that required that either drilling
  127│
  128│operations begin or a delay rental payment to be made within 12 months of execution. Compl. ¶ 54.
  129│
  130│In Count VII of their complaint, Plaintiffs seek declaratory relief holding that the Griffith lease expired on its own terms, on account of paragraph 4, which required that either drilling operations begin or a delay rental payment to be made within 12 months of execution. Compl. ¶ 59.
  131│
  132│## III. DISCUSSION OF LAW
  133│
  134│### A. THE STANDARD FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT.
  135│
  136│Summary judgment is appropriate when “there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(a). The Supreme Court of the United States has explained that Rule 56 requires “the threshold inquiry of determining whether there is the need for a trial—whether, in other words there are any genuine factual issues that properly can be resolved only by a finder of fact because they may reasonably be resolved in favor of either party.” *Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc.*, 477 U.S. 242, 250 (1986). In making such an inquiry, the court should consider the evidence in the light most favorable to the non-moving party. *Krumheuer v. GAB Robins N. Am., Inc.*, No. 10-4396, 2012 WL 1700702, at \*3 (6th Cir. May 16, 2012) (internal citations omitted). “The mere existence of a scintilla of evidence in support of the plaintiff’s position will be insufficient” to justify denial of the motion, *Donald v. Sybra, Inc.*, 667 F.3d 757, 763 (6th Cir. 2012) (quoting *Anderson*, 477 U.S. at 252); in order to prevail, rather, the party opposing summary judgment must offer “significant probative evidence.” *King v. Pennsylvania Life Ins. Co.*, No. 10-1672, 2012 WL 975077, at \*5 (6th Cir. Mar. 23, 2012) (quoting *Anderson*, 477 U.S. at 248). In short, the Court
  137│
  138│must determine “whether there is enough evidence for a jury to decide for the non-movant before denying a summary judgment motion.” *Id.* (citing *Anderson*, 477 U.S. at 252).
  139│
  140│### **B. AS MASON DIXON HAS ASSIGNED ALL OF ITS INTERESTS IN THE CAMERON AND GRIFFITH LEASES, IT HAS NO RELATIONSHIP UPON WHICH EQUITABLE RELIEF CAN BE GRANTED.**
  141│
  142│An assignment involves a transfer of property from one party to another. *W. Broad Chiropractic v. Am. Family Ins.*, 912 N.E.2d 1093, 1095 (Ohio 2009) (internal citation omitted); 3 Ohio Jur. 3d *Assignments* § 1 (2006) (footnote omitted). As a result, the assignee “acquires” these rights, and the rights of the assignor are “extinguished.” 6 Am. Jur.2d, *Assignments* § 1 (2012) (footnote omitted). In essence, the assignee “stands in the shoes of the assignor” and “succeeds to all the rights and remedies of the [assignor].” *Inter Ins. Exch. of Chi. Motor Club v. Wagstaff*, 59 N.E.2d 373, 375 (Ohio 1945).
  143│
  144│In *Ford Motor Credit Co. v. Ryan*, 939 N.E.2d 891 (Ohio App. 10th Dist., 2010), the appellate Court affirmed summary judgment in favor of a defendant on contract-related claims because the defendant had assigned its rights to another party. *Id.* at 921. In that case, Ford Motor Credit Company (“Ford”) sued two parties for failing to make payments on a motor-vehicle lease agreement. *Id.* at 899. When the two lessors filed counterclaims against Ford, they joined the dealer from whom they had acquired the vehicle in question. *Id.* at 901. Based on an unassailed affidavit by the dealer’s president stating that the retail installment contract had been assigned to Ford, however, the Court concluded that the dealer did not retain any interest in the contract, and affirmed summary judgment in its favor. *Id.* at 921.
  145│
  146│In this case, Mason Dixon has proven through the attached affidavit that its interests in the Griffith and Cameron Leases were assigned to Marquette Exploration, LLC. Count I of the
  147│
  148│Complaint concerns what kind of activity is permitted under the Griffith and Cameron leases. Counts II, IV, and V concern whether the leases are invalid, in whole or in part. Counts VI and VII concern whether the leases have expired. Count III seeks to avoid future unjust enrichment on the part of the lessee.
  149│
  150│All of the Counts seek relief, both equitable and in damages, which could only be awarded against the present lessees of the Griffith and Cameron leases. Indisputably, that is not Mason Dixon. In light of the complete assignment of interests, Mason Dixon has no present rights with respect to the property covered by these leases, nor any interests to be impacted by a ruling on the present validity of the leases.
  151│
  152│### **C. UNJUST ENRICHMENT IS NOT A VALID CAUSE OF ACTION UNDER THE CIRCUMSTANCES.**
  153│
  154│The elements of an unjust-enrichment claim are as follows: (1) a benefit conferred by a plaintiff upon a defendant, (2) knowledge by the defendant of the benefit, and (3) retention of the benefit by the defendant under circumstances in which it would be unjust to do so without payment. *City Rentals, Inc. v. Kesler*, 191 Ohio App.3d 474, 2010-Ohio-6264, 946 N.E.2d 785, ¶ 12, citing *Hambleton v. R.G. Barry Corp.* (1984), 12 Ohio St.3d 179, 183, 12 OBR 246, 465 N.E.2d 1298.
  155│
  156│*Warnecke v. Chaney*, 956 N.E.2d 908 (Ohio App. 3rd Dist., 2011). Unjust enrichment is an equitable cause of action available only under a quasi-contract, i.e. a contract that is implied-in-law. *Williams v. Goodyear Aircraft Corp.*, 85 N.E.2d 601, 604 (Ohio App. 9th Dist., 1948); 17 C.J.S. *Contracts* § 6 (2012). Claims of unjust enrichment and breach of contract are mutually exclusive. *Arcade Co. Ltd. v. Arcade, LLC*, 105 F. App'x 808, 811 (6th Cir. 2004).
  157│
  158│In Count III of their complaint, Plaintiffs allege that
  159│
  160│the oil and natural gas deposits within the Marcellus, Utica and Trenton shale formations are worth hundreds of millions to billions of dollars in profits for defendants. Given the unequal bargaining positions and knowledge of defendants, jointly and severally, held during the formation of the Lease agreements with each and every class member, defendants, jointly and severally,
  161│
  162│would be unjustly enriched via the retention of such enormous profits without payment of just compensation to all class members.
  163│
  164│Compl. ¶ 35. Nowhere in the Complaint is it alleged that defendants, or any one of them, has generated any profits to date as a result of the oil and gas rights held under the Leases. In fact the above-quoted paragraph of the Complaint frames Plaintiffs' unjust enrichment claims only in future terms: Plaintiffs allege the mineral *deposits are worth millions to billions of dollars in profits* and that retention of such profits by defendants *would* constitute unjust enrichment. There is no allegation that defendants have, as yet, extracted minerals and reaped such profits. In fact, upon information and belief, to date there has been no such extraction on the subject property.
  165│
  166│Given all of this, as to Mason Dixon, the unjust enrichment count should be dismissed on either of the following grounds: First, a claim for unjust enrichment cannot, as a matter of law, be asserted for damages which are the subject of a written lease – under applicable law, the only valid claim for such damages (in this case royalties, which are covered by the lease) would be a breach of contract claim. Second, because it is indisputable that Mason Dixon no longer has rights to the oil and natural gas deposits within the shale formations subject to the Leases, they consequently have no right to profits from such mineral deposits and consequently, no way in which to allegedly become unjustly enriched by such profits. Mason Dixon accordingly requests this Court to grant summary judgment in its favor on Count III.
  167│
  168│## IV. CONCLUSION
  169│
  170│When a lessee assigns all of its rights under a lease to another, that assignee/lessee entirely replaces the original lessee with respect to all aspects of the lease. To allow the lessor to
  171│
  172│pursue contract-related claims against the original lessee, as the Plaintiffs want to do in this matter against Mason Dixon, violates the very principle and purpose of assignment.
  173│
  174│WHEREFORE, based upon the foregoing, the Defendant, Mason Dixon Energy, Inc., respectfully requests this Court enter an Order awarding it summary judgment on all counts in Plaintiffs' Complaint.
  175│
  176│Dated this 18th day of March, 2013.
